strengths: Addresses a highly practical and significant challenge in robot learning: personalizing frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to identify and manipulate specific, user-designated objects without retraining or fine-tuning.

Proposes a simple, training-free, yet highly effective two-stage adapter pipeline (Visual Attentive Prompting) combining instance-level visual grounding with pixel-space highlighting and instruction rewriting.

Provides a thorough empirical validation across two newly established simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER and Personalized-VLABench) as well as a real-world physical robot setup, consistently outperforming strong baselines.

Includes a deep and insightful analysis of alternative personalization strategies, particularly showing why token-learning (soft prompt) baselines fail to achieve reliable end-to-end control due to spatial attention dilution in VLA action heads.
Excellent presentation, clear visual illustrations, and a detailed breakdown of failure modes (visual prompt errors, cross-view inconsistencies, and manipulation failures).
weaknesses: The method is heavily reliant on the performance of individual off-the-shelf vision modules (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2). Upstream errors in these perception models directly propagate to the control loop, as highlighted in the error analysis.
The instruction rewriter relies on simple template-matching ('my X' to 'the [tint] X'), which may be brittle when handling more complex, free-form, or non-templated user commands.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical and high-impact problem: enabling general-purpose Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to manipulate specific user-owned instances ('my cup') without requiring expensive per-object fine-tuning.

Proposes an elegant, training-free adapter framework (Visual Attentive Prompting) that elegantly bridges the instance-to-category gap by combining non-parametric visual retrieval, open-vocabulary detection, pixel-level color highlighting, and template-based instruction rewriting.

Extremely thorough evaluation across multiple robot embodiments (Google Robot, WidowX, Franka, and SO-101) in both simulation (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) and physical real-world environments.

Provides a deep, high-quality analysis of token-learning baselines. The study on why VLM-learned concept tokens transfer successfully in embedding space (via CKA and kNN@1 metrics) but fail to guide low-level closed-loop actions due to attention dilution in VLA action heads is a highly valuable scientific insight.
Outstanding writing, clear figures, and a transparent and constructive error-case analysis that categorizes and quantifies failures across different benchmarks.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on upstream visual modules: If the initial open-vocabulary detection or representation-based matching fails, or if tracking drifts across frames or cameras, the incorrect prompt propagates downstream, leading to consistent failure.

The instruction-rewriting mechanism relies on template-based string replacement (e.g., matching 'my X' and replacing with 'the [color] X'), which may be brittle or fail to generalize to complex, non-standard, or highly conversational phrasing.

Evaluation is currently limited to tabletop, single-object, short-horizon tasks (pointing or picking). Scaling to multi-step long-horizon routines with multiple personal objects remains an open challenge.

strengths: Addresses an important and highly practical problem in robotics: personalizing general-purpose, language-conditioned Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to manipulate specific user objects (e.g., "my cup") among visually similar distractors.
Proposes a completely training-free, modular framework (VAP) that adapts frozen VLAs at test-time without requiring any gradient updates or parameter fine-tuning on new objects.

Provides a thorough and diverse empirical evaluation spanning two simulation platforms (Personalized-SIMPLER and Personalized-VLABench) as well as physical experiments on a real 6-DoF SO-101 robot arm across multiple categories.

Includes rigorous comparisons with competitive baselines (such as a token-learning/soft-prompt baseline adapted from Yo'LLaVA) along with deep-dive analyses of token embedding alignment and cross-attention heatmaps.
weaknesses: Limited Technical Novelty: The proposed Visual Attentive Prompting (VAP) framework is essentially a pipeline assembly of existing, off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO for detection, DINOv2 for feature matching, SAM2 for tracking, and pre-trained VLAs). The high-level concept of utilizing visual highlights or masks to guide robot control has been widely studied in prior works (e.g., MOKA, Roboground, PIVOT).

Fragility and Cascading Errors: Because VAP relies on a strictly sequential, training-free perception-to-control pipeline, any matching or tracking errors in the early stages propagate directly to the controller. The downstream VLA has no mechanism to recover if the upstream matching locks onto a distractor.

Lack of Multi-view Consistency: In multi-view VLA scenarios (which are standard for setups like VLABench and the real-world robot), the per-view grounding is performed independently. This leads to severe cross-view inconsistencies (Case 2 failures), which account for more than 50% of the overall failures. The paper leaves the resolution of this critical multi-view alignment challenge to future work.

Brittle Instruction Rewriting: The language rewriting relies on rigid template-based string matching (e.g., replacing 'my X' with 'the [tint-color] X'). This assumption is highly restrictive and would likely fail on natural, complex, or indirect user commands.

Insufficient Ablation on Prompting Styles: The manuscript lacks a thorough analysis/ablation of how different visual prompting styles (e.g., tint opacity, alternative colors, solid masks, or bounding boxes) affect the internal visual features and control stability of the frozen VLA backbones.

strengths: Highly practical and well-motivated setting: Addressing instance-level personalization in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models without retraining is an important, high-impact problem for household robotics.

Training-free and lightweight design: Visual Attentive Prompting (VAP) leverages pre-existing vision models (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2) to perform input-space interventions, making it highly compatible with any frozen VLA backbone and extremely fast to deploy.

Exceptional evaluation and benchmarking: The authors adapted two simulation benchmarks (SIMPLER and VLABench) and validated their system on a physical SO-101 robot arm across multiple tasks (selection and pick-and-place), showing massive gains in success rate (SR) and correct movement ratio (CMR).

Rigorous baselines and deep analysis: The paper includes a very strong set of baselines, including a well-optimized soft-prompt (token learning) baseline. The analysis on why token learning fails for closed-loop control (attention drift and dilution in the VLA trunk) is highly insightful and adds significant scientific value.

Excellent presentation and thoroughness: The paper is beautifully written, well-structured, and includes comprehensive error analyses (Case 1/2/3 breakdown), runtime latency measurements, and extensive ablations of every design choice.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on upstream perception models: Because the system is training-free, any failure in open-vocabulary detection, reference embedding matching, or tracking directly propagates to the VLA, as analyzed in the multi-view inconsistency failures (Case 2).

Rule-based instruction rewriting: The language rewrite mechanism relies on a deterministic template-based strategy ('my X' -> 'the [color] X'). While sufficient for the evaluated benchmarks, complex or highly conversational instructions might require an LLM-based parsing step.

strengths: Formulates a highly practical and under-explored challenge in robotic learning: instance-level personalization of frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models using only a few reference images.

Proposes an elegant, training-free, and modular perception-action adapter (VAP) that leverages off-the-shelf visual models (DINOv2, Grounding DINO, SAM2) to successfully guide frozen VLAs via visual highlighting and text-rewriting.

Provides a thorough and rigorous empirical evaluation across two simulated environments (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) and physical real-world experiments on an SO-101 tabletop robotic arm.

Includes a highly sophisticated comparison with strong baselines, including a token-learning (Soft Prompt) approach where token embeddings are transferred from VLM to VLA and visualized through spatial attention heatmaps.

Presents clear and honest failure mode categorizations and detailed ablation studies (such as mask vs. bounding box, template rewriting, and voting rules) that offer valuable insights for future research.
weaknesses: Highly dependent on the performance of upstream open-vocabulary object detectors and tracking models; cascading failures in grounding directly propagate to the VLA policy's manipulation actions.

The instruction rewriting mechanism is largely rule-based ('my X' to 'the [tint-color] X'), which might limit flexibility under more complex or highly diverse natural language instructions without an auxiliary LLM parser.

In multi-view setups, the per-view grounding is factorized independently, occasionally leading to cross-view inconsistencies (e.g., highlighting a target in one view but a distractor in another). While a cross-view association formulation is mathematically sketched, its implementation is left to future work.

strengths: Addresses a highly practical and significant problem in robotics: enabling instance-level personalization for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models without requiring expensive per-object retraining or fine-tuning.

The proposed Visual Attentive Prompting (VAP) is elegant, training-free, and simple to implement, successfully bridging the gap between semantic understanding and instance-level control through combined visual masks and text rewriting.

The evaluation is exceptionally thorough, spanning two simulation platforms (Personalized-SIMPLER and Personalized-VLABench) as well as real-world physical robot experiments across multiple categories and tasks.

The paper includes highly rigorous baselines, notably a very detailed analysis of a token-learning baseline (adapted from Yo'LLaVA) with deep dives into embedding space preservation (CKA, kNN@1) and spatial attention visualization.

Includes a comprehensive error analysis that classifies failures into clear categories (such as multi-view inconsistency) and outlines concrete mathematical formulations for future work to address these issues.
weaknesses: The instruction rewriting mechanism relies on a deterministic, rule-based approach (mapping 'my X' to 'the [color] X'), which may be brittle when handling more diverse, conversational, or indirect user language.

As noted in the paper's failure analysis, the independent per-view tracking strategy is susceptible to cross-view inconsistencies (Case 2), where different cameras highlight different objects under occlusion, leading to unstable actions.

The technical contribution is primarily a system-level integration of existing off-the-shelf vision and tracking components (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM 2) rather than a novel model architecture or learning paradigm.
There is a confusing reference on page 16 to the use of 'GPT-5.1' for generating textual descriptions, which does not correspond to currently released public models.
